title: Finite-Particle Quantum Reduction of Thermodynamic Irreversibility
abstract: Thermodynamics is useful because it lets us predict and control complex systems from a few accessible quantities when microscopic reconstruction is impractical. We ask whether this operational reduction can be less costly in a finite quantum system than in a matched classical one. We compare a few-boson Bose--Hubbard chain with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart under the same driving and the same coarse spatial record. The quantum system relaxes more in the observed particle distribution, yet the retained mean energy resolves more of the microscopic structure hidden by that record, leaving less information unusable and smaller entropy generation. We then close the process into a heat-engine cycle whose controls use only the measured mean energy and spatial record, not full state tomography; at matched thermal resources, the smaller entropy generation gives more work and higher efficiency. The advantage fades as the particle number grows toward the classical-field regime.
summary: This work compares the thermodynamic irreversibility of a finite-particle quantum system (Bose-Hubbard model) against its classical field analog. By analyzing entropy generation during a heat-engine cycle, the authors show that retaining energy information beyond just the spatial record allows the quantum system to perform work with lower entropy cost. This quantum advantage, however, vanishes in the large particle number limit.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the operational reduction of information in a finite quantum system, compared to its classical counterpart, leads to a less costly thermodynamic process regarding entropy generation.
main_result: The quantum system exhibits smaller entropy generation and achieves higher work efficiency than the classical system under matched thermal resources, although this advantage diminishes as the particle number increases toward the classical limit.
method: The analysis uses a heat-engine cycle comparison, quantifying information loss via entropy gaps derived from comparing state representations constrained by the spatial record (R) versus the combined energy and record (E, R).
model_or_system: The study compares a finite-particle Bose–Hubbard chain (quantum system) with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart. The Hamiltonians are matched by setting specific coupling constants.
key_observables: Entropy generation ($\Sigma$), work extracted, information gaps ($G_R, A_E, I_{E,R}$), and the comparison of $\Sigma_Q$ vs $\Sigma_{cl}$.
important_parameters: Total number of bosons ($Q$), number of sites ($L$), and the confinement parameter ($\Lambda$).
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes matched thermal resources, and the advantage of the quantum system is shown to fade as $Q$ grows.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the matched quantum-classical construction, showing the three state representations ($ho,  ar{ho}_R,  ar{ho}_{E,R}$) and the corresponding entropy gaps, while supplementary figures confirm numerical stability and robustness.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by defining the quantum and classical models, develops the theoretical framework using entropy decomposition identities ($G_R = A_E + I_{E,R}$), applies this to a heat-engine cycle comparison, and concludes by analyzing the resulting entropy costs and their dependence on particle number.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative comparison of quantum vs. classical thermodynamics in the context of finite, non-equilibrium processes, directly addressing the role of quantum coherence in thermodynamic efficiency.
